prompt.context_jp: 富士浅田のビジネスホテル___、午後の日ざしのなかで しんと静まっていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 富士浅田のビジネスホテル___、午後の日ざしのなかで しんと静まっていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits the opening scene-setting line.

feedback.correct_en: This sentence opens the scene by presenting the hotel as the setting we're going to talk about — a classic topic use of は. The hotel is already known as the workplace from earlier chapters.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would frame the hotel as newly introduced information, as if answering 'what was quiet?'. Here the narration is describing an already-established setting.

contrast_examples.en: (As for) the hotel, it was quiet. — setting the scene
It was the hotel that was quiet. — identifying which place

prompt.context_jp: フロントに立つ 遠藤清美の隣で、由美___「相談があるんですけど」と切り出したのは…
prompt.prompt_jp: 由美___「相談があるんですけど」と切り出した
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits Yumi suddenly piping up next to Kiyomi?

feedback.correct_en: が marks Yumi as the one who, out of the blue, started the conversation — this is new, event-reporting information inside a relative clause ending in のは.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make Yumi the ongoing topic, but the sentence is zooming in on the moment she acted, not continuing a topic about her.

contrast_examples.en: Yumi was the one who brought it up. — event focus
As for Yumi, she brought it up. — ongoing topic

prompt.context_jp: 「だって 謎___多すぎません？」
prompt.prompt_jp: 謎___多すぎません？
prompt.prompt_en: Yumi is explaining why Takahashi seems alien-like.

feedback.correct_en: The adjective 多い describes a quality — in this exclamatory 〜すぎません? pattern we point out that 'mysteries' are what there is too much of. が naturally marks the thing being evaluated.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would set 'mysteries' up as a topic to be commented on, which sounds flat and unnatural in this surprised, pointing-out tone.

contrast_examples.en: There are a lot of mysteries. — natural
As for mysteries, there are a lot. — contrastive, needs a follow-up

prompt.context_jp: 高橋さん___ どこに住んでるとか 家族のこととか 誰も知らなくないですか？
prompt.prompt_jp: 高橋さん___ どこに住んでるとか…
prompt.prompt_en: Inside the embedded question 'where Takahashi lives'.

feedback.correct_en: Inside a subordinate clause like '〜が住んでる(か)', the subject typically takes が, not は. は tends to stay in the main clause as the overarching topic.
feedback.incorrect_en: 高橋さんは would try to make Takahashi the topic of the whole sentence, but here he's only the subject of the embedded 'where he lives' clause.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼がどこに住んでるか知らない。
contrast_examples.en: I don't know where he lives. — subject inside embedded clause

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は家族のことを話さない。
contrast_examples.en: He doesn't talk about his family. — main-clause topic

prompt.context_jp: 「ちなみに その 高橋さん宇宙人説ってさ 由美ちゃん___言ってるだけだよね」
prompt.prompt_jp: 由美ちゃん___言ってるだけだよね
prompt.prompt_en: Kiyomi is pointing out who alone is spreading the alien theory.

feedback.correct_en: This is exhaustive-listing が: 'it's only Yumi (and nobody else) who's saying it'. The 〜だけ reinforces that identification.
feedback.incorrect_en: 由美ちゃんは would make Yumi a topic ('as for Yumi, she's just saying it'), losing the sharp 'only you' nuance Kiyomi is poking at.

contrast_examples.jp: 由美ちゃんが言ってるだけ。
contrast_examples.en: It's only Yumi who's saying it. — identifies the sole source

contrast_examples.jp: 由美ちゃんは言ってるだけ。
contrast_examples.en: Yumi is just saying it (and not doing anything). — topic + 'merely'

prompt.context_jp: はっちが得意げにたどっていた矢印___、そこで ふつりと途切れている。
prompt.prompt_jp: はっちが得意げにたどっていた矢印___、そこで ふつりと途切れている。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle sets up 'the arrow' as the thing the sentence comments on?

feedback.correct_en: The relative clause already picks out a specific arrow; the main clause then comments on it ('…breaks off there'). This 'identified-then-commented-on' structure takes は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would newly introduce the arrow, but it has already been described in detail by the relative clause — the sentence's job is to say what happens to it.

contrast_examples.en: The line he drew is thin. — comment on a specified thing
The line is thin. — new observation

prompt.context_jp: 高橋の力を借りたい人間___、身近にもう一人いたらしい。
prompt.prompt_jp: 高橋の力を借りたい人間___、身近にもう一人いたらしい。
prompt.prompt_en: A narrator sentence introducing a new petitioner for Takahashi's help.

feedback.correct_en: The point of the sentence is that such a person EXISTS ('いた'). Existential/presentational sentences introduce a new referent and use が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would presuppose we already know this person and are now commenting on them — but the narration is just now revealing their existence.

contrast_examples.jp: もう一人いる人がいた。
contrast_examples.en: There was another person. — new existence

contrast_examples.jp: その人はもう一人いた。
contrast_examples.en: That person existed another time. — odd without known referent

prompt.context_jp: ふだん___気弱に見える高橋も、こと自分の身の安全がかかると 徹底して自分を擁護しにかかる。
prompt.prompt_jp: ふだん___気弱に見える高橋も…
prompt.prompt_en: A pivot: 'normally' timid, BUT when his own safety is at stake…

feedback.correct_en: This is contrastive は: 'normally he looks timid, (but in this situation he doesn't).' は on a time-adverb highlights the implicit contrast with the exceptional case.
feedback.incorrect_en: が doesn't attach to adverbs like ふだん here and would break the contrast setup that the second clause depends on.

contrast_examples.jp: ふだんは優しいけど、今日は厳しい。
contrast_examples.en: Usually he's kind, but today he's strict. — classic contrastive は
Today is special. — topic/contrast on time

prompt.context_jp: 高橋___まだ戻らない。
prompt.prompt_jp: 高橋___まだ戻らない。
prompt.prompt_en: Three people are waiting in the car for Takahashi.

feedback.correct_en: Takahashi is the already-established figure everyone is waiting for; the sentence comments on his state. That's prototypical topic は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present Takahashi as newly entering the scene, but he's exactly who everyone has been watching for — he's the ongoing topic.

contrast_examples.en: Takahashi still isn't here (we know who he is).
Takahashi has come! — new arrival, event report

prompt.context_jp: 湯呑みを置く動きにも、そこはかとない不満___にじんでいる。
prompt.prompt_jp: そこはかとない不満___にじんでいる。
prompt.prompt_en: Narration describing a subtle feeling that 'bleeds out'.

feedback.correct_en: The sentence newly observes that discontent is appearing in his movement — a descriptive sensing of something emerging. That's new-information が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would set 'the discontent' up as a known topic, but here the narrator is just now noticing it seeping out.

contrast_examples.jp: 顔に疲れがにじんでいる。
contrast_examples.en: Fatigue is bleeding into his face. — descriptive, が
That fatigue can't be hidden. — already known

prompt.context_jp: 校舎を囲む雑木林___、かつて濫伐で ずいぶん薄くなったと聞いていた…
prompt.prompt_jp: 校舎を囲む雑木林___、かつて濫伐で ずいぶん薄くなった…
prompt.prompt_en: The narrator starts describing a visible feature of the surroundings.

feedback.correct_en: The relative clause already picks out which thicket — 'the thicket surrounding the school'. The sentence then makes a general comment about it. That setup is topic は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would turn the thicket into newly spotlighted information, but we're being told what the narrator knows about an already-defined thing.

contrast_examples.jp: この森は昔もっと深かった。
contrast_examples.en: This forest used to be deeper. — comment on known thing
A forest is spreading out. — descriptive observation

prompt.context_jp: 財布と鍵___掴んで玄関に立つと、清美は もう一つ思い出したように 若葉を振り返った。
prompt.prompt_jp: 財布と鍵___掴んで玄関に立つと…
prompt.prompt_en: What particle marks the things being grabbed?

feedback.correct_en: 掴む is a transitive verb — the thing being grabbed is marked with を.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make the wallet/keys the subject (nonsensical here), and に would read as 'to/at the wallet'.

contrast_examples.en: To hold a key.
The key fell. — subject

prompt.context_jp: 数日が経ち、清美と高橋は仕事帰り___ はっちの部屋へ 呼び出されていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 清美と高橋は仕事帰り___ はっちの部屋へ 呼び出されていた。
prompt.prompt_en: 'On their way home from work' — what marks this time circumstance?

feedback.correct_en: 仕事帰りに is a set time-expression meaning 'on the way home from work' — に pins it as the timing of the event.
feedback.incorrect_en: で would read as 'by means of coming home from work', and を doesn't fit a time phrase here.

contrast_examples.en: Drop by on the way home from school.
Wait at school. — location

prompt.context_jp: 「うん… 今のは 由美ちゃん___ 1人で言ってるだけだからさ」
prompt.prompt_jp: 由美ちゃん___ 1人で言ってるだけだからさ
prompt.prompt_en: Kiyomi explains why Yumi's 'urban legend' doesn't count.

feedback.correct_en: が identifies Yumi as the sole speaker — 'it's just Yumi alone saying it'. The 1人で reinforces this exclusive identification.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would weaken the point by making Yumi a topic rather than pinpointing her as the only source.

contrast_examples.en: He decided it alone (identifies the sole doer).
As for him, he decided it alone. — less pointed

prompt.context_jp: 高橋の目は 図の一点___止まっていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 図の一点___止まっていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Where his eyes stopped — pick the location particle.

feedback.correct_en: With 止まる meaning 'come to rest at (a spot)', the point of rest is marked with に — a point-of-arrival/location nuance, not an activity location.
feedback.incorrect_en: で marks the place where an activity happens, but 止まる here isn't an activity — it's a state of resting at a point. を would mean 'passing through'.

contrast_examples.en: The gaze fixates on one point. — point of rest
Stop (while moving) in the park. — activity location

prompt.context_jp: 都市伝説と言われても清美には___がつかず、ただ次のひとことを 待つほかなかった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 清美には___がつかず
prompt.prompt_en: She had no clue what Yumi meant.

feedback.correct_en: 見当がつく (lit. 'an estimate forms') is the set phrase for 'to have a clue / to guess'. Its negative 見当がつかない means 'to have no idea'.
feedback.incorrect_en: 気がつく means 'to notice' — different meaning. 目がつく isn't a standard idiom.

contrast_examples.en: I have no idea.
I didn't notice.

prompt.context_jp: 清美は___を挟まず、まずは説明を最後まで聞くことにした。
prompt.prompt_jp: 清美は___を挟まず
prompt.prompt_en: She decided not to interrupt.

feedback.correct_en: 口を挟む literally 'to insert one's mouth' is the standard idiom for 'to butt in / interrupt a conversation'.
feedback.incorrect_en: 手を挟む would be physically pinching one's hand; 耳を挟む isn't an idiom (小耳に挟む 'overhear' exists, but is a different construction).

contrast_examples.en: To butt into a conversation.
To overhear.

prompt.context_jp: やり取りが尽きたのか、高橋は 深く息を___ 天井を見上げた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 高橋は 深く息を___ 天井を見上げた。
prompt.prompt_en: He let out a deep sigh.

feedback.correct_en: 息を吐く means 'to breathe out / exhale / sigh'. Combined with 深く, it conveys the deep exhale of resignation Takahashi shows here.
feedback.incorrect_en: 息を吸う means 'to inhale' (opposite direction), and 息を入れる is not idiomatic for a sigh — it suggests taking a break.

contrast_examples.en: To let out a sigh.
To inhale deeply.

prompt.context_jp: 「はっちのために ___ 脱ぎますか」
prompt.prompt_jp: はっちのために ___ 脱ぎますか
prompt.prompt_en: 'Let's lend a helping hand for Hacchi.'

feedback.correct_en: ひと肌脱ぐ literally 'take off one layer of skin', idiomatically 'to pitch in / help out' for someone's sake. Perfectly fits the 'we'll help Hacchi' moment.
feedback.incorrect_en: ひと息 pairs with つく ('take a breather'), ひと言 with 言う ('say a word') — neither combines with 脱ぐ.

contrast_examples.jp: 友達のためにひと肌脱ぐ。
contrast_examples.en: To go out of one's way for a friend.
To take a breather.

prompt.context_jp: 交渉は こじれ、部屋には 気まずい沈黙が___。
prompt.prompt_jp: 部屋には 気まずい沈黙が___。
prompt.prompt_en: 'An awkward silence fell over the room.'

feedback.correct_en: 沈黙が落ちる is the literary collocation for 'silence falls' — the same metaphor as English.
feedback.incorrect_en: 沈黙が降る isn't idiomatic in Japanese (though 'rain falls' uses 降る), and 沈黙が来た would just be flat and unnatural.

contrast_examples.en: A heavy silence fell.
Rain fell. — different verb for different nouns

prompt.context_jp: それでも息を___ていることは 隠しきれていない。
prompt.prompt_jp: 息を___ていることは 隠しきれていない。
prompt.prompt_en: Takahashi can't fully hide that he's out of breath.

feedback.correct_en: 息を切らす is the fixed idiom 'to be out of breath / gasping' — exactly what someone looks like after sneaking in and out of a building.
feedback.incorrect_en: 息を止める means 'to hold one's breath' (deliberate), and 息を吸わす isn't idiomatic here.

contrast_examples.jp: 息を切らして走ってきた。
contrast_examples.en: He came running, out of breath.
To hold one's breath.

prompt.context_jp: ___も積もれば山となるとはよく言ったもので、夜な夜な描き足してきたらしい印は もはや紙の余白を覆い尽くしていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: ___も積もれば山となる
prompt.prompt_en: The famous proverb being invoked here is…

feedback.correct_en: 塵も積もれば山となる ('even dust piled up becomes a mountain') is the standard proverb for 'small things accumulate into big ones' — fitting Hacchi's nightly scribbles.
feedback.incorrect_en: 雪 and 砂 don't form this proverb; they'd sound like made-up variants.

contrast_examples.jp: 塵も積もれば山となる。
contrast_examples.en: Many a little makes a mickle.
A journey of a thousand miles begins with one step. — related but different

prompt.context_jp: 「しかも あそこ 俺の___だからね」
prompt.prompt_jp: あそこ 俺の___だからね
prompt.prompt_en: Takahashi reveals his personal connection to the school.

feedback.correct_en: 母校 means 'alma mater' — the school he once attended, which is exactly the extra sting of the trespassers vandalizing it.
feedback.incorrect_en: 母国 is 'homeland (country)' — too big in scale. 実家 is 'family home' — not a school.

contrast_examples.en: This is my alma mater.
To go back to one's family home.

prompt.context_jp: Scene-opening narration about the hotel being quiet in the afternoon.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds more natural as a scene-opening description?

choices.text: 富士浅田のビジネスホテルは、午後の日ざしのなかで しんと静まっていた。
富士浅田のビジネスホテルが、午後の日ざしのなかで しんと静まっていた。

feedback.correct_en: Scene-setting narration prefers は, which positions the hotel as the already-shared stage we're commenting on. The actual story uses this version.
feedback.incorrect_en: The が version sounds like you're pointing at the hotel for the first time among several candidates — jarring at a chapter opening.

contrast_examples.en: The town was asleep. — natural narration
It was the town that was asleep. — needs context to justify

prompt.context_jp: Kiyomi casually explains how she heard about Takahashi's family.
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds more natural in this casual exchange between coworkers?

choices.text: いや 普通に本人が話してたけど
いいえ、普通にご本人がお話しになっていましたが

feedback.correct_en: The chapter's casual back-and-forth between Kiyomi and Yumi uses plain forms and 普通に as a filler — the actual line (a).
feedback.incorrect_en: The keigo version (ご本人, お話しになる) would be bizarre between close coworkers chatting about a mutual friend — register-mismatched.

contrast_examples.en: He himself told me. — casual peers

contrast_examples.jp: ご本人がお話しになっていました。
contrast_examples.en: He himself was speaking of it. — polite about a superior

prompt.context_jp: Takahashi protests that if he doesn't go in, he can't be caught.
prompt.prompt_en: Which casual-speech form matches the moment's natural rhythm?

choices.text: そもそも入んなきゃ 捕まんないからね
そもそも入らなければ 捕まらないからね

feedback.correct_en: In this fast, exasperated back-and-forth, Takahashi uses the colloquial contractions 入んなきゃ / 捕まんない — matching the real line.
feedback.incorrect_en: The fully formal 入らなければ / 捕まらない isn't wrong grammar, but it sounds stiff and out of character for an irritated gripe.

contrast_examples.jp: 行かなきゃ分かんない。
contrast_examples.en: You won't know unless you go. — casual

contrast_examples.jp: 行かなければ分からない。
contrast_examples.en: Same meaning, careful speech.

prompt.context_jp: The three are waiting in the car; the narrator notes that Takahashi still hasn't come back.
prompt.prompt_en: Which short narrator line sounds more natural here?

feedback.correct_en: Everyone has been waiting for Takahashi — he's a shared, known subject. Topic は gives this quiet beat of narration its natural feel.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would sound like Takahashi is just being pointed out, which clashes with the fact he's already the focus of everyone's attention.

contrast_examples.en: He still isn't here. — comment on known person
Someone isn't coming. — ambiguous subject

prompt.context_jp: Takahashi, somewhat offended, explains that the symbol the vandals drew is extremely obscene on his home planet.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing fits Takahashi's casual, slightly worked-up tone?

choices.text: あのマーク ウチの星では 超卑猥なマークだからね
あのマークはウチの星において非常に卑猥なマークであります

feedback.correct_en: The real line keeps the casual, spoken rhythm: topicless 'あのマーク', 超 as a colloquial intensifier, and ending 〜だからね for emphasis.
feedback.incorrect_en: The alternative sounds like a stiff written statement — 〜において and 〜であります don't match an animated after-mission chat with coworkers.

contrast_examples.en: It's super bad, you know. — casual

contrast_examples.jp: 非常に危険であります。
contrast_examples.en: It is extremely dangerous. — stiff/formal
